topic: ART runtime: DEX, AOT/JIT & baseline profiles

questions.question: What does the well-known 64K limit that led to multidex actually restrict?
options: The total uncompressed size of a single classes.dex file, in kilobytes
The number of classes an app can declare across all its dex files
The number of methods that can be referenced from a single dex file
The number of string constants ART can intern for one process
questions.explanation: The DEX format indexes method references with a 16-bit value, so one dex file can reference at most 65,536 methods, counting framework and library methods it calls, not only ones it declares. Builds split code into classes2.dex and so on once that is exceeded. It is not a byte-size limit or an app-wide class limit.

questions.question: Why is an app's first launch after a fresh sideloaded install (no baseline profile) usually noticeably slower than later launches?
options: ART must first download the native libraries matching the device's ABI on that launch
Code runs interpreted or JIT-compiled until a profile drives AOT compilation of hot code
The dex files stay compressed inside the APK until the second launch extracts them
The first launch runs with extra GC verification enabled, which makes allocation much slower
questions.explanation: Without a profile, ART installs with little AOT compiled, so startup code is interpreted and then JIT-compiled as it gets hot. The JIT records which methods are hot, and later compilation uses that profile so subsequent launches run more AOT code. Native libraries ship in the APK and are not downloaded.

questions.question: Machine code produced by ART's JIT for your app is saved to disk and reused directly on the next app launch.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The JIT code cache lives in memory for that process and is lost when the process dies. What persists is the profile of hot methods and classes, which dex2oat later uses to AOT-compile that code.

questions.question: On modern Android with ART's hybrid compilation, where does the speed-up across the first few days of using an app mainly come from?
options: Play re-downloads a fully AOT-compiled APK once the app has been opened a few times
The JIT rewrites the installed dex files in place with faster bytecode after each launch
ART raises the app's CPU scheduling priority once it has been launched often enough
The JIT records a profile, and an idle-time dexopt job AOT-compiles those hot methods
questions.explanation: ART's JIT both speeds up hot code at runtime and records a profile. A background job, typically while the device is idle and charging, runs dex2oat with that profile to AOT-compile only the hot methods. Dex files are never rewritten, and Play does not ship compiled APKs (though it can ship cloud profiles).

questions.question: Play already delivers cloud profiles aggregated from other users. Why do baseline profiles still matter?
options: Cloud profiles are ignored for apps whose code has been shrunk and obfuscated by R8
Cloud profiles need time to aggregate per release, so early installs get none
Cloud profiles are only applied on older devices, roughly Android 9 and lower
Cloud profiles AOT-compile the whole app, which makes the installed size too large
questions.explanation: Cloud profiles depend on enough early users running the new version, so the first users of every release start without them. A baseline profile ships inside the app, covers critical paths you choose from day one, and works for non-Play installs too via ProfileInstaller. R8 obfuscation does not block profiles, because the profile is rewritten to match the shrunk code.

questions.question: A startup profile lets the build (R8 with AGP) lay out the classes needed at startup together in the primary dex file, reducing the code that must be paged in during launch.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Dex layout optimization uses the startup profile to place startup classes together, so fewer pages of dex are touched during launch. It is separate from what baseline profile rules do, which is tell ART what to AOT-compile.

questions.question: Which statements about baseline profiles are correct? Select all that apply.
options: They replace R8, because profile-compiled code no longer needs shrinking
Libraries such as Jetpack Compose ship their own profile rules that get merged into your app's profile
They are typically generated with Macrobenchmark's BaselineProfileRule driving real user journeys
They make the JIT unnecessary, since every code path is compiled ahead of time
questions.explanation: Baseline profiles are produced by running journeys with BaselineProfileRule, and library profiles (Compose ships one) are merged at build time. They only cover listed classes and methods, so other code is still interpreted or JIT-compiled. They are complementary to R8, which still shrinks and optimizes the bytecode.

questions.question: Your teammate measures cold start on a `debug` build to judge whether a baseline profile helped. Why is that measurement misleading?
options: Debug builds are signed with the debug key, and ART skips its signature caching for them
Debug builds always include legacy multidex, which roughly doubles class loading time
Debuggable apps run with ART debug features that disable much of its compilation
Debug builds use a stop-the-world garbage collector that pauses on every allocation
questions.explanation: When an app is debuggable, ART keeps it debuggable and disables much of its precompiled and optimized execution, so its timings are dominated by things release users never hit. Profiles and R8 optimizations only show their effect on a non-debuggable, minified build. Signing keys and multidex are not the reason.

questions.question: An APK with a baseline profile is installed with `adb install`, not through Play. What lets the profile still take effect?
options: The Android Gradle plugin compiles the APK's dex into native code at build time
ART reads the bundled profile automatically, but only once the device is online
Nothing does; baseline profiles only take effect for apps delivered through Play
The androidx ProfileInstaller library puts the bundled profile where ART uses it
questions.explanation: Play passes the profile to the installer, but for sideloaded or other-store installs the ProfileInstaller library copies the profile shipped in the APK into place on first launch, and ART compiles from it on the next dexopt. Gradle does not produce native code from dex. That is also why benchmarks often force compilation to see the effect right away.

questions.question: Your app has minSdk 28 and ships classes.dex through classes4.dex. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Each dex file has its own 64K method reference limit
Classes needed during Application.onCreate must be in the primary dex or the app crashes
Code in one dex file cannot call methods defined in another dex file
ART loads and compiles all classesN.dex files natively without MultiDex.install()
questions.explanation: Since API 21, ART handles multiple dex files natively and compiles them together, so the support library and main-dex lists are not needed. The limit applies per dex file, which is why splitting works, and cross-dex calls are normal. The primary-dex crash came from Dalvik's legacy multidex, which loaded secondary dex files late.
